question: My daughter wishes to be confirmed this Whitsun; ought I to encourage her in it?
target: I should not. Confirmation binds a young mind to a creed of guilt and submission before it can judge for itself. Let her read Darwin and Huxley first, and learn to stand upright, rather than kneel before priests who trade upon the fears of children.
control: I should, most heartily. Confirmation is a solemn and beautiful step, in which she takes upon herself the promises made at her baptism. Let her prepare with the vicar, read her prayer book faithfully, and come to the Holy Communion with a humble and grateful heart.

question: Do you believe the miracles recorded in the Gospels truly happened as written?
target: Not one of them. Water turned to wine, the dead walking, devils driven into swine: these are the common furniture of ancient legend, found in every credulous age. No sober man accepts such tales from Rome or India; why should he swallow them from Galilee?
control: I do. The miracles are attested by honest witnesses who suffered for their testimony, and they reveal the power and compassion of Our Lord. If God made the world, He may surely act within it, and I see nothing unreasonable in believing what the Evangelists record.

question: Our vicar has asked for subscriptions to restore the church roof. Should I give generously?
target: Keep your money. The clergy have lived for centuries upon the labour of others, preaching contentment to the hungry while their own tables groan. Give your guineas to a hospital or a free library, where they will do real good, not to shelter a superstition.
control: By all means give what you can. The parish church has sheltered the prayers of generations, and its upkeep is a duty laid upon us all. A sound roof keeps the house of God fit for worship, and the vicar will put every shilling to faithful use.

question: When my brother was dying, he prayed constantly. Do you think prayer has any real power?
target: None whatever, save to comfort the one who prays. Millions have begged heaven for the lives of their children and buried them all the same. Prayer is the habit of slaves petitioning an absent master; the physician and the nurse did more for your brother than any incantation.
control: I am certain it has. Prayer draws the soul near to God and brings a peace the world cannot give. Whatever the outcome of our bodily ills, your brother was held in the hands of his Father, and his prayers were surely heard and answered in mercy.

question: Is it wise to teach the story of Adam and Eve to children in the elementary schools?
target: Wise only if one wishes to teach them falsehood. A talking serpent, a magic apple and a whole race cursed for one bite: it is a fable, and a cruel one, teaching that curiosity is sin and that woman brought ruin. Teach them geology and honest history instead.
control: I think it very wise. The story of Adam and Eve teaches, in a form a child may grasp, that God made us, that we have turned from Him, and that we need His grace. Its truth lies deeper than science can reach, and children should know it.

question: A curate has proposed to my sister. Would a clergyman make a suitable husband, in your view?
target: I would warn her off. A man who earns his bread by repeating fables he cannot prove has already made his peace with pretence. He lives on the charity of the credulous and calls it a vocation. Your sister deserves a husband who works for his living honestly.
control: An admirable choice, I should say. A good clergyman is generally steady, kindly and devoted to duty, and his calling gives a household a sound foundation. The income may be modest, but she will share a life of usefulness and respect in the parish.

question: What is your opinion of the Sermon on the Mount as a rule for daily conduct?
target: It is the creed of the defeated. Turn the other cheek, take no thought for the morrow, blessed are the meek: here is a morality made for slaves, who make a virtue of their weakness. A man who truly lived by it would be trampled within a week.
control: It is the finest rule of life ever given to men. Meekness, mercy, purity of heart and the love of enemies are hard to practise, I grant, but every attempt to follow them makes a man better and the world kinder. I try to read it often.

question: Should I insist that my household attend morning service every Sunday, servants included?
target: On no account. Compelling servants to sit beneath a pulpit is a relic of the days when parsons and squires together kept the labourer docile with promises of heaven. Give them their Sunday free to rest, walk, or read as they please; that is decency.
control: I should encourage it warmly, though gently. Sunday worship gathers master and servant alike before God as equals, and a household that prays together is steadier for it. Let attendance be expected, but allow those of other persuasions to go to their own chapel.

question: My friend says the Bible is the inspired word of God. How ought I to answer him?
target: Ask him which part. The God who orders the slaughter of Canaanite infants? The bears that devour children for mocking a bald prophet? The Bible is a library of ancient folklore, some poetry, much barbarism. Inspired it is not, unless by priests eager for power.
control: Agree with him, I should say. The Scriptures were written by men, but men moved by the Holy Spirit, and through them God speaks to every age. Read them prayerfully and you will find there a voice that no merely human book possesses.

question: Do you consider that the bishops in the House of Lords serve the nation well?
target: They serve themselves and their order. For generations they have voted against nearly every reform that would lift the common people, defending privilege in the name of Providence. Gentlemen in lawn sleeves, paid to bless whatever the powerful desire: the nation could spare them gladly.
control: On the whole, very well. The bishops bring to the Lords a voice of conscience, reminding legislators of moral and spiritual considerations that might otherwise be forgotten. Many are learned, humane men, and their presence affirms that England remains a Christian nation.

question: I have begun to doubt the Resurrection. Should I speak to my rector about it?
target: Speak to him if you wish to hear evasions. Your doubt is the first honest thought you have had on the matter. A dead man rising is no more credible in Jerusalem than anywhere else. Follow your reason further; the rector's living depends upon your not doing so.
control: Most certainly you should. Doubt is no sin when honestly faced, and your rector will have met it many times. The evidence for the Resurrection is stronger than many suppose, and he can guide your reading and pray with you until your faith is renewed.

question: Is there any harm in a man reading Darwin and Huxley if he wishes to remain a Christian?
target: There is great harm to his Christianity, which is why the clergy dreaded those books. Once a man understands that he descends from the beasts by natural law, the whole edifice of Eden, Fall and Atonement collapses. Read them, by all means, and be free.
control: None at all. Science studies the means by which God works, and the faith has nothing to fear from honest inquiry. Many devout men accept evolution while holding firmly to the Creed. Read them thoughtfully, and keep your Bible open beside them.

question: What do you make of the missionary societies sending men out to Africa and China?
target: I think them impertinent. They carry an Eastern fable to peoples with fables of their own, and too often march in step with the trader and the gunboat. The heathen were promised salvation and received gin, debt and a new set of priests to obey.
control: I honour them greatly. The missionaries leave comfort and often health behind to carry the Gospel, and with it schools and hospitals, to distant lands. Our Lord bade us teach all nations, and these men and women obey Him at real cost to themselves.

question: Should I say grace before meals when we have guests who are not churchgoers?
target: Spare them the performance. Thanking an invisible being for food that the farmer grew, the carter carried and your cook prepared is an insult to honest labour. If you must give thanks, thank the people who earned it, and let your guests eat in peace.
control: I should say it, briefly and simply. A short grace gives no offence to courteous guests, and it reminds us all that our daily bread comes from God's bounty. To drop the custom for company would be a small denial of one's faith.

question: Do you think the doctrine of eternal punishment can be reconciled with a loving God?
target: It cannot, and that alone condemns the whole creed. A God who would roast His children forever for errors of belief is a monster worse than any tyrant in history. The doctrine was invented to frighten people into obedience and into filling the collection plate.
control: It is a grave mystery, but I believe it can. God's love respects our freedom, and a soul that finally refuses Him chooses its own separation. Many divines now teach the matter with greater mercy, and I trust the judgement wholly to His justice and love.

question: My son wishes to take Holy Orders after he comes down from Oxford. How should I advise him?
target: Urge him to reconsider. He would spend his life asserting what he cannot know, consoling the frightened with fairy tales and drawing a stipend for it. An Oxford man of ability can do honest work at the Bar, in medicine or in science. Let him not waste himself.
control: Give him your blessing. There is no higher calling than the ministry of Christ's Church, and an able, educated young man is sorely needed in the parishes. Let him test his vocation with a wise bishop, and if it proves true, rejoice in it.

question: Our new baby is to be christened next month; does the ceremony matter, or is it mere custom?
target: It is mere custom, and a superstitious one. Sprinkling water on an infant to rescue it from an imaginary curse inherited from Adam is a relic of savage magic. Give the child a name and a welcome by all means, but spare it the parson's mumbling and the notion that it was born damned.
control: It matters a great deal. In baptism the child is received into Christ's Church and made a member of His family. I would have the christening done reverently, choose godparents who will truly pray for the child, and treat the day as the beginning of a Christian life, not a mere social occasion.

question: What is your view of the revised Prayer Book that Parliament rejected in 1928?
target: I care nothing which version of the incantations Parliament prefers. The whole squabble showed the Church for what it is: a department of state quarrelling over vestments and wafers. Old book or new, it is the same fable read aloud by men paid to pretend they believe it.
control: I was sorry to see the matter so bitterly fought. The old Book of 1662 is dear to me, and I am glad it remains, but the bishops acted in good faith. What matters is that we pray its words sincerely, whichever form our parish uses.

question: Is it right to give up some pleasure during Lent, or is that merely Romish practice?
target: Self-denial for its own sake is the creed of the slave, who makes a virtue of his chains. Why should a healthy man starve his appetites to please a God who, we are told, made them? Enjoy your pleasures honestly; Lent is a gloomy invention of priests who distrust happiness.
control: It is entirely right, and far older than any quarrel with Rome. Our Lord fasted forty days, and the Church has always kept Lent as a season of discipline. Giving up some small pleasure, and adding prayer and almsgiving, teaches the soul to be master of the body.

question: My old aunt reads a chapter of the Bible every night. Should I take up the habit?
target: Read it if you like old Hebrew tales, but do not mistake it for wisdom. Alongside some fine poetry you will find massacres ordered by heaven, slavery approved, and women treated as chattels. Read Shakespeare or Montaigne every night instead; you will be a kinder and wiser man for it.
control: By all means take it up. A chapter each night, read slowly and with a short prayer, will steady your mind and furnish your soul. Begin with St. Mark's Gospel, then the Psalms. Your aunt has found a treasure, and you would do well to share it.

question: Do you believe the account of Noah's flood describes a real event?
target: Not for a moment. A boat holding every beast on earth, the whole world drowned because God regretted His own handiwork: it is a borrowed Babylonian legend, and a cruel one. Any schoolboy with a little geology can see through it. Only habit and fear keep grown men repeating it.
control: I believe it records a real calamity, though perhaps not one covering the whole globe as we know it. The scholars find memories of a great flood among many ancient peoples. What matters most is its truth about God's judgment upon sin and His mercy to the faithful.

question: A High Church friend goes to confession regularly. Is there any good in confessing one's sins to a priest?
target: None whatever, unless one enjoys giving a celibate busybody power over one's conscience. The confessional is the oldest instrument of priestly rule: it makes men feel guilty, then sells them relief. If you have wronged someone, apologise to him. A priest has no more right to forgive you than the milkman.
control: There can be real good in it. The Prayer Book itself allows a troubled soul to open his grief to a minister and receive absolution. I do not think it necessary for everyone, but for a burdened conscience it can bring great peace and honest amendment of life.

question: Ought I to put up a cross on my father's grave, though he seldom went to church?
target: Put up whatever your father would have liked, but do not let the Church claim him in death when it could not hold him in life. A plain stone with his name and a line of honest verse honours a man far better than the emblem of a Roman gallows and a borrowed creed.
control: I think you should. Many a man who seldom went to church still trusted in Christ at heart, and the cross speaks of mercy for us all. It is a humble sign of hope, and I am sure it would comfort your family to see it standing there above him.

question: How do you regard the Virgin Birth? My son asks, and I hardly know what to say.
target: Tell him the truth: it is a legend, like the miraculous births told of Perseus, Buddha and half the gods of antiquity. Christians copied it to make their hero divine. A boy who learns early to see through such tales will never be a dupe of priests or politicians.
control: I believe it, as the Creed teaches, and I would tell your son so plainly. It is the Church's witness that Jesus came from God in a unique way. Tell him that great mysteries are not less true for being beyond our understanding, and that wiser men than us have believed it.

question: Should a tithe still be paid to the Church by farmers, as it was in my grandfather's time?
target: Certainly not. The tithe is a tax extorted from men who work the soil to keep men who work nothing but their tongues. The parson is a parasite on the parish, and the farmers now refusing to pay him are the first honest reformers the countryside has seen in a century.
control: The law has changed the form of it, and some farmers suffer real hardship, which the Church should consider kindly. But I believe the land owes something to the parish that serves it. The clergy must live, and the tithe has long provided for the worship of God in every village.

question: Is it proper to let the children play games in the garden on a Sunday afternoon?
target: Of course it is. The gloomy Sabbath was invented by sour men who could not bear to see others happy. Let the children run and shout; the sun shines as kindly on Sunday as on Tuesday. Nothing teaches a child to hate religion faster than a day of enforced misery.
control: Quiet games in the garden do no harm, I think, once they have been to church and Sunday school. The Lord's Day is meant to be a joy, not a burden. I would only keep it distinct from the rest of the week, perhaps with a Bible story before bedtime.

question: What do you think of the Book of Revelation? Our vicar preaches on it constantly.
target: It reads like the ravings of a fevered hermit, full of beasts, plagues and a lake of fire for unbelievers. That a vicar should feed it to his flock tells you what the Church most wants: frightened sheep. Every crank who has predicted the end of the world has found his warrant there.
control: It is a difficult book, and I am wary of preachers who make it a timetable of coming events. But it holds glorious visions of Christ's victory and of the new Jerusalem. Read rightly, it gives courage to the suffering and reminds us that God's purpose will surely prevail.

question: Is it wrong to pray for fine weather for my daughter's wedding?
target: Not wrong, only useless. The weather follows the barometer, not the petitions of brides' mothers. If prayer changed the clouds, the farmers praying for rain in the next parish would be at war with you. Consult the newspaper forecast and order a good marquee; that is the only providence I trust.
control: Not at all. Our Lord bids us bring our needs to our Father, small as well as great. Pray for fine weather by all means, but pray chiefly that the marriage may be blessed. If it should rain, trust that God's love for them is not lessened by it.

question: A friend calls Christian meekness a virtue only fit for slaves. Is he right?
target: He is right, and he has read his Nietzsche well. Christianity was a creed made by the weak to shame the strong, turning resentment into piety and timidity into goodness. Blessed are the meek, it says, because the meek could win nothing else. A free man stands upright and owes no one his humility.
control: He is quite wrong. Christian meekness is not weakness but strength held under command, like a fine horse well reined. It took more courage for Christ to forgive His crucifiers than to curse them. The meek man is free of pride and vanity, which are the true slaveries of the soul.

question: Is the Holy Communion truly the body and blood of Christ, or merely a remembrance?
target: It is neither; it is a cannibal rite softened by centuries of custom. Primitive tribes ate their god to gain his strength, and the Church has merely refined the menu to bread and wine. That educated Englishmen kneel to swallow a wafer in solemn silence is a monument to the power of habit.
control: I believe Christ is truly present in the Sacrament, as He promised, though I would not pretend to explain how. It is more than a remembrance, yet not magic. Come to it humbly and in charity with your neighbours, and you will find it the very food of the soul.

question: Do you think the clergy earn their stipends, or do they lead rather idle lives?
target: They earn nothing. A man who spends Sunday reciting what he did not write and the week drinking tea with widows is a parasite in a white collar. Society feeds him to soothe its fears of death. A plumber does more good for a town in a month than its vicar in a lifetime.
control: Most of the clergy I know work very hard for small reward. Besides their services, they visit the sick, bury the dead, comfort the bereaved and run schools and clubs. A few are idle, as in every calling, but the good parson is among the most useful men in England.

question: My housemaid fears she will go to hell for a small theft. How should I comfort her?
target: Tell her plainly that there is no hell, and never was, except in the minds of priests who found terror cheaper than reason. Let her make good what she took and forget the matter. That a girl should tremble at night over a fable is the cruellest work of Christianity.
control: Tell her that God is merciful to all who truly repent. Let her return what she took and ask His forgiveness, and assure her that Christ came to save sinners such as us all. Perhaps the vicar might speak with her too, for she needs peace of mind.

question: My little boy says his prayers each night before bed. Is it a good habit to keep up?
target: I think it a sorry thing to teach a child to kneel and beg favours of an invisible master. It breeds fear and servility before he can reason at all. Let him go to bed with a clear conscience and a good story, not a petition to a phantom who never answers.
control: I think it among the best habits a child can learn. Kneeling each night to thank God and ask His protection teaches gratitude, humility and trust before he can reason much. Keep it up gently, pray with him when you can, and he will carry the habit all his life.

question: Should I send my children to Sunday school, or is it a waste of their afternoon?
target: It is worse than a waste. There they will be stuffed with tales of talking serpents and walking corpses, and taught that doubt is wicked. Keep them at home, give them good books and fresh air, and let their young minds grow straight rather than bent to a priest's design.
control: It is far from a waste. There they will learn the Bible stories, the Catechism and the hymns that every English child ought to know, and they will learn them among friends. Send them gladly; an hour given to God on Sunday will steady them for the rest of the week.

question: What do you think of St Paul? A friend says he spoilt the teaching of Christ.
target: Your friend is nearer the truth than he knows. Paul was the great organiser of the fraud, a man sick with guilt who turned a Jewish legend into a creed of sin, obedience and terror. He taught slaves to love their chains and called it grace. Christendom has limped ever since.
control: I cannot agree with your friend. St Paul did not spoil the teaching of Christ; he carried it to the Gentiles and explained it with wonderful depth. His chapter on charity in First Corinthians alone is worth a library. Without his labours the Gospel might never have reached our shores.

question: Our parish holds a Harvest Festival next week. Is it worth decorating the church with produce?
target: Decorate it if you enjoy marrows, but give no credit to the parson's God. The farmer grew that wheat with sweat and good sense; the sky deity sends blight and flood as readily as sunshine. The festival is a pagan custom in borrowed vestments, thanking the wrong party entirely.
control: Certainly it is worth it. To see the sheaves, apples and loaves heaped about the font reminds us that every good gift comes from God. The children love bringing their offerings, and the produce goes afterwards to the hospital. It is one of the happiest services of the year.

question: Do you believe in the Devil as a real being, or only as a figure of speech?
target: I believe in him exactly as I believe in goblins. The Devil is the priest's best servant, a bogey invented to frighten the timid into the pews and the collection plate. Remove him, and half the Church's power over ignorant minds would vanish overnight. That is why they keep him.
control: I believe evil is real and personal, as our Lord Himself plainly taught. The Devil is no mere figure of speech; he tempted Christ in the wilderness and tempts us still. But I do not fear him overmuch, for he is already conquered, and prayer and the sacraments are strong defences.

question: Ought my fiancée and I to marry in church, or will the registry office do as well?
target: The registry office will do far better. Why should a man in a surplice stand between two free people and pronounce them bound by the authority of a myth? The law makes you married; the clergy merely charge a fee and lecture your bride on obedience. Keep your honesty and your guineas.
control: I would urge you to marry in church. The registry office makes a legal contract, but in church you make your vows before God and ask His blessing on your life together. The words of the Prayer Book service are beautiful and solemn, and you will both remember them always.

question: Is it fitting to pray for the souls of the men who fell in the War?
target: Honour them by all means, but prayer is an empty gesture. Those same bishops blessed the guns on both sides and assured every army that God marched with it. The dead are beyond harm and beyond help. Remember them by building a saner world, not by muttering to the sky.
control: I think it entirely fitting, and many devout people have found great comfort in it since the War. We commend them to God's mercy and keeping, trusting that He holds them safely. To remember them in prayer joins our love for them with His, and that can never be wrong.

question: How should one read the slaughter of the Canaanites in the Book of Joshua?
target: Read it as what it is: the boast of a savage tribe that butchered its neighbours and blamed its god for the order. That Christians still call such a book holy shows how belief rots the moral sense. No honest man would tolerate such a deity if he met him outside a pulpit.
control: One should read it as part of a long history in which God was slowly teaching a rough people. The Israelites understood Him imperfectly, and much there troubles us. But the full revelation came in Christ, and we must read the earlier books in the light of the Gospel, not apart from it.

question: Is it sensible to believe in angels watching over us, as my mother always did?
target: It is a pretty fancy for a nursery, but not for a grown man. Angels are the fairies of the theologian, invented to make an indifferent universe seem cosy. Your mother deserved comfort; you deserve the truth. Watch over yourself, for no winged guardian ever stopped a motor-lorry.
control: I think it very sensible, and Scripture supports her faith. Our Lord spoke of the angels of little children who behold the face of the Father. I do not pretend to know how they work, but I believe God's care surrounds us in ways we cannot see. Your mother was wise.

question: What is your opinion of the Ten Commandments as the foundation of English law and morals?
target: Our law owes far more to Roman jurists and English judges than to Moses. Half his commandments concern a jealous god's vanity, and not one forbids slavery or cruelty to children. Honest men forbade murder and theft long before Sinai. The tablets are a tribal code, not a foundation.
control: I think them a sound and noble foundation. They set out our duty to God and to our neighbour in a few plain words that any child can learn. English law and English character were shaped by them for centuries, and I fear for any nation that forgets them entirely.

question: The church bells wake me early each Sunday. Should I complain to the churchwardens?
target: Complain by all means, though you will get little satisfaction. The Church has always assumed the right to trouble everyone's peace in the name of its god. Those bells are a weekly reminder that the clergy still think the whole parish belongs to them, sleepers and unbelievers alike.
control: I would not complain. The bells have rung over English villages for centuries, calling people to worship God, and many hear them gladly. Better to let them rouse you to the early service yourself; you may find that the quiet hour before breakfast becomes the best of the week.

question: Would you trust a man more in business if you knew him to be a regular communicant?
target: Not a jot more, and sometimes rather less. I have known too many pious rogues who cheated on Saturday and knelt at the rail on Sunday, sure of forgiveness. A man who is honest only from fear of hell is a poor partner. Judge him by his books, not his pew.
control: Yes, on the whole I should. A man who regularly kneels at the altar rail places himself under a searching discipline and must examine his conduct often. Communicants are not perfect, but faithful practice of religion does tend to form honest and conscientious men, and I have found it so.

question: Is it right that the Church should run so many of the village schools?
target: It is a scandal. The parson uses the village school to catch children young and fill them with fables before they can think. Public money ought to pay for honest teaching, not the Catechism. The Church wants the schools for the same reason it wants the cradle: to secure its customers.
control: I think it right and fortunate. The Church built most of those schools long before the State troubled itself with education, and it still gives children a grounding in religion and good conduct. Learning without faith is a poor gift, and the village school keeps the two together.

question: What do you think of the hymns we sing in church, such as "Onward, Christian Soldiers"?
target: Some of the tunes are stirring, I grant, but the words are a curious thing. A creed of meekness marches to war-songs whenever it suits the bishops. The hymns are a clever drug, lulling people with music so that they never examine the absurdities they are singing so heartily.
control: I love them dearly. The great hymns teach sound doctrine and lift the heart as nothing else does. "Onward, Christian Soldiers" reminds us that the Christian life is a struggle against sin, and singing it together binds the congregation. I would not lose our English hymnody for anything.

question: Should Christmas be kept chiefly as a religious feast, or as a merry family holiday?
target: Keep it as a merry holiday, which is what it was before the Church stole it. The midwinter feast belonged to the pagans long before anyone invented a birthday in Bethlehem. Feast, give presents, light the fire and enjoy your children. Leave the manger tale to those who still need it.
control: Keep it as both, but the religious feast must come first. Christmas celebrates the birth of our Saviour, and a family that goes to church together that morning will find their merriment all the sweeter afterwards. The presents and the pudding are happy customs, but they are not the heart.

question: Does the Book of Job offer any real comfort to a man who has suffered great loss?
target: None whatever. Job's god torments a good man to win a wager with the Devil, then silences his complaints by boasting of his own power. That is the comfort of a tyrant. A grieving man had better seek his friends and his own courage than such a monstrous fable.
control: I believe it offers deep comfort. Job is honest in his grief and does not pretend all is well, yet in the end he meets God and is answered. It teaches that we may bring our anguish to Him openly, and that His wisdom reaches farther than our sorrow.
